title: Elevator Implementation
description: Implement elevator state machines with event-driven architecture, handle concurrent requests safely, and build comprehensive testing strategies.

segments.text: The elevator state machine has five core states: idle, moving_up, moving_down, door_open, and emergency_stop. Transitions are triggered by events: floor_request, floor_reached, door_timer_expired, and emergency_signal. Encoding these as an explicit state machine — not nested if-else chains — makes the logic auditable, testable, and extensible.

Event-driven architecture decouples input from processing. Floor buttons, cabin buttons, weight sensors, and door sensors all produce events. An event queue serializes them. The state machine consumes events one at a time, updating state and producing actions — move motor, open door, update display. This eliminates concurrency bugs in the core logic.

Multiple floor buttons pressed simultaneously generate concurrent events. The event queue naturally serializes them. But the scheduling algorithm must handle batch arrivals — re-evaluate the optimal path after each new request rather than just appending. Use a priority queue sorted by the current scheduling algorithm to maintain the request order.

Door logic is surprisingly complex. Open on arrival, start a timer. If someone enters — detected by weight change or light beam — reset the timer. If door is blocked for more than thirty seconds, sound an alarm. Never close the door while weight is increasing. In emergency, override all door logic and open immediately.

The elevator is on floor 10 going up with requests for floors 15 and 20. While passing floor 12, a new request comes in for floor 8 going down. Should the elevator continue up or reverse? This decision affects three passengers. What logic do you implement?
segments.thought_prompt: Should the elevator reverse for a floor 8 request while going up to floors 15 and 20? Justify your decision.

segments.text: Motor control abstracts physical movement into three operations: accelerate, maintain_speed, and decelerate. The deceleration distance depends on current speed and elevator weight. Begin decelerating N floors before the target to stop precisely. Overshoot is dangerous — the elevator must level with the floor within five millimeters for safe boarding.

Test the state machine exhaustively: every state, every valid transition, every invalid transition that should be rejected. Use property-based testing — generate random event sequences and verify invariants hold: the elevator never moves with doors open, weight capacity is never exceeded, emergency stop is always reachable from any state.

Simulation testing generates realistic traffic patterns — morning rush, lunch, evening rush — and runs the scheduling algorithm against them. Measure average wait time, maximum wait time, and energy consumption across thousands of simulated hours. Compare algorithm variants quantitatively rather than arguing theoretically.

Elevator systems must handle hardware failures gracefully. Motor sensor failure: stop at nearest floor and open doors. Weight sensor failure: refuse to close doors as a safety measure. Communication failure with central controller: fall back to standalone LOOK scheduling. Every failure mode needs a safe default behavior — the elevator must never become a trap.
Design the complete class hierarchy and state machine for an elevator system. What are your core classes, their responsibilities, and how do they interact through the event-driven architecture?
segments.thought_prompt: Design the class hierarchy: Elevator, Controller, Scheduler, Door, Motor. How do they communicate?

segments.text: Elevator implementation is a masterclass in state machine design. Event-driven architecture eliminates concurrency bugs, explicit state machines make logic auditable, property-based testing catches edge cases, simulation validates performance, and fail-safe defaults handle hardware failures. The code structure mirrors the real-world safety requirements — correctness over cleverness.
